content: The use of antibiotics as a prophylactic measure to prevent postpartum endometritis in women who delivered vaginally and were free from infection has been studied, but the evidence remains inconclusive. A trial conducted in Zambia evaluated the impact of midwife home visits on the health of mothers and their full-term newborns following normal vaginal delivery. These visits, conducted at 3, 7, 28, and 42 days postpartum, aimed to assess health problems and breastfeeding behaviors. During each visit, lasting approximately one hour, mothers were asked about their perceptions of their own and their baby’s health, any observed health issues, and actions taken in response to symptoms. Breastfeeding patterns and the availability of social support at home were also discussed. The midwife examined both the mother and infant, providing care, counseling, advice, and medical treatment as needed. A study in the USA involving 107 women reported perineal wound complications at two weeks postpartum among those who experienced thirdor fourth-degree perineal tears during vaginal delivery. However, none of the trials reviewed reported cases of sepsis or maternal deaths, and the reporting of other outcomes was inconsistent. The evidence from four small trials on infection prevention was insufficient to draw reliable conclusions about the benefits and risks of prophylactic interventions, including their timing. One trial suggested that a single dose of 2 grams of intravenous antibiotics administered one hour after delivery might reduce endometritis, but further data is required before recommending this practice. Consequently, the panel decided not to recommend routine antibiotic prophylaxis following uncomplicated vaginal delivery for the prevention of puerperal sepsis. Instead, women should be counseled on maintaining hygiene, particularly hand hygiene, during the postnatal period. For women with thirdor fourth-degree perineal tears, prophylactic antibiotics were recommended to prevent perineal wound complications. Puerperal sepsis remains a significant cause of maternal morbidity and mortality. Basic hygienic practices are effective in preventing sepsis and pose no harm. However, the use of medications, including antibiotics, during the postnatal period may carry risks for the newborn. Concerns about the inappropriate use of antibiotics in this period were also noted. Psychosocial support provided by trained personnel is recommended for women at high risk of postpartum depression, although the evidence supporting this recommendation is of very low quality. Routine formal debriefing for all women to reduce the risk of postpartum depression is not recommended due to insufficient evidence. Health professionals should provide opportunities for women to discuss their birth experiences during their hospital stay. Women who have experienced the loss of a baby should receive additional supportive care. A systematic review of 31 studies involving 19,224 women examined interventions to prevent postpartum depression. These studies, conducted in middleand high-income settings, included drug therapies, professional support, peer support, debriefing, educational interventions, and combined approaches. Depression was measured using various tools, with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) being the most commonly used. The evidence for many interventions was inconclusive. No effect was reported for postnatal antidepressant or progestogen interventions. Some evidence suggested that professional support interventions might reduce depression in at-risk women at six weeks, four months, and six months postpartum. Debriefing interventions showed potential benefits at three weeks and three months postpartum, but the evidence quality was very low. Peer support and educational interventions demonstrated some effect at three months postpartum but not at six months or beyond. Overall, the quality of evidence was assessed as low or very low, with most studies being small, unblinded, and conducted in developed countries. The panel emphasized the importance of informing women and their families about potential mood changes in the postpartum period, which are often transient and resolve within 10–14 days. Persistent symptoms should be evaluated. WHO has published guidance on interventions for mental disorders in non-specialized health settings. Stigma associated with mental health problems may deter women from seeking professional care. Medications and professional psychological support have cost implications. The panel identified significant knowledge gaps requiring further research. These include evaluating the effectiveness of postnatal care packages, optimal timing of discharge, strategies for implementing postnatal care recommendations, and approaches to providing psychosocial support. Research is also needed on maternal depression epidemiology, tools for identifying depression’s contribution to suicide, and prevention strategies. Other priorities include evaluating interventions to prevent sepsis, care for small babies, and strategies to prevent hypothermia. Developing algorithms to identify sick newborns during postnatal care and assessing newborn danger signs that families can recognize are also critical areas for research. The ultimate goal of these guidelines is to improve the quality of postnatal care and health outcomes for mothers and newborns. Dissemination and implementation of the guidelines are essential and will involve collaboration with international partners, WHO offices, ministries of health, and other organizations. The guidelines will be published on the WHO website, and a policy brief will be developed for policymakers, program managers, and clinicians. Existing WHO publications on postnatal care will be revised, and training packages will be updated. The recommendations will be incorporated into community-level tools and service standards for newborn and maternal care. Successful implementation will require well-planned, participatory processes to adapt the guidelines to local contexts and health service needs.
